_readme: SOUTH CAROLINA CIVIL DEADLINE RULES -- 9 rows, SCRCP 12, 33, 34 and 36.
== THE E-MAIL QUESTION IS UNRESOLVED, AND THE DEFAULT IS DELIBERATE ====
READ THIS BEFORE WIDENING THE EXTENSION. A web search returns, as Rule
6(e), a sentence extending the five days to e-mail service. THAT SENTENCE
IS NOT IN RULE 6(e). The rule was read verbatim from sccourts.org and
contains no e-mail language at all:
(e) Additional Time After Service by Mail or Upon Statutory Agent.
Whenever a party has the right or is required to do some act or take
some proceedings within a prescribed period after the service of a
notice or other paper upon him and the notice or paper is served upon
him by mail or upon a person designated by statute to accept service,
five days shall be added to the prescribed period.
The 2022 Supreme Court order `RE: Service by E-Mail in the Trial Courts`
(Appellate Case No. 2022-000029, 6 May 2022, signed by all five justices)
was then read end to end: paragraphs (a) through (f) -- purpose, e-mail as
an additional method, service on lawyers, service by and on
self-represented litigants, requirements, proof of service -- and NO
time-extension provision whatsoever.
SO ON THE TWO PRIMARY SOURCES ACTUALLY READ, WHETHER THE FIVE DAYS REACH
E-MAIL IS UNRESOLVED. It may live in a later order this pass did not find.
THE DIRECTION DECIDES THE DEFAULT: if e-mail does collect the five days
and the engine omits them, the date is EARLY -- safe. If it does not and
the engine adds them, the date is LATE -- the direction that misses a
filing. So `sc_rcp_6_e` extends for MAIL and STATUTORY AGENT only.
DO NOT WIDEN IT ON THE STRENGTH OF A SEARCH SUMMARY.
This is the Tennessee lesson in a third form. There, a time rule reading
`by mail` was WIDENED by a deeming provision in the service rule. Here a
search result claims the same widening and the primary sources do not
support it. Same instinct -- check the service materials -- opposite
outcome.
== FIVE DAYS, NOT THREE, AND THE RULE SAYS WHY =========================
Rule 6(e)'s own drafting Note: `This Rule 6(e) is the same as the Federal
Rule except that the additional time to take an act after service is by
mail is INCREASED FROM 3 TO 5 DAYS.` Every seeded state adds three except
California's and New York's per-method tables and New Jersey's five. A
three-day extension carried from a neighbour computes TWO DAYS EARLY on
every mailed South Carolina period.
IT ALSO REACHES SERVICE UPON A STATUTORY AGENT -- `or upon a person
designated by statute to accept service` -- which no other seeded rule
does. That is its own method here, not a variety of mail.
== THE FIRST STATE-PLUS-FEDERAL HOLIDAY UNION ==========================
Rule 6(a) rolls the last day `unless it is a Saturday, Sunday OR A STATE
OR FEDERAL holiday`. Every jurisdiction seeded before this keys on one
list, or on two STATE lists (Wisconsin). Here the federal list is a
CO-EQUAL SOURCE, and it is not optional: JUNETEENTH AND COLUMBUS DAY ARE
FEDERAL HOLIDAYS AND ARE NOT IN S.C. Code § 53-5-10. A state-only calendar
misses both and reports EARLY. Both are asserted by the generator.
The calendar also carries two state-only days no other seeded
jurisdiction has -- CONFEDERATE MEMORIAL DAY (10 May, fixed) and THE DAY
AFTER THANKSGIVING, in the statute itself -- and a THREE-DAY CHRISTMAS
BLOCK (24, 25 and 26 December) that COLLIDES under the § 53-5-30 shift in
2026, 2027 and 2028. See tools/gen_sc_calendar.py; in 2027 Christmas Day
itself is not an emitted date at all.
TWO § 53-5-30 CAVEATS ARE RECORDED, NOT RESOLVED, and both belong with the
bundled holiday question: the section is captioned `effect on presentment
of bills, notes, and checks` and shifts `for all of the purposes
aforesaid`, so whether it reaches COURT deadlines is arguable; and it
shifts only the STATE half, the federal half having 5 U.S.C. § 6103(b) --
CHECKED to be identical, so one rule serves both.
== THE 'MAY' / 'SHALL NOT BE REQUIRED' SPLIT -- GEORGIA'S DISTINCTION ==
South Carolina has exactly Georgia's split, and it decides the row shape.
RULES 33 AND 34 SAY `a defendant MAY serve` within 45 days after service
of the summons and complaint. That is a PERMISSIVE ALTERNATIVE running
from a DIFFERENT EVENT, not a floor on the 30-day period. So each gets its
OWN PLAIN ROW and the engine never chooses between them -- choosing would
need to know both dates AND that the party is a defendant, and there is no
party-role field.
RULE 36 SAYS `a defendant SHALL NOT BE REQUIRED to serve answers or
objections before the expiration of 45 days`. That IS a mandatory floor,
so it is a `resolve_periods: later_of` with different counts per limb --
the shape built after Georgia's O.C.G.A. 9-11-36(a)(2) shipped FIFTEEN
DAYS EARLY.
THE TWO WORDINGS ARE CLOSE ENOUGH TO READ ACROSS AND THEY MEAN OPPOSITE
THINGS. Treating 33/34 as floors would compute LATE for a defendant who
did not take the alternative; treating 36 as an option would compute EARLY
and, since Rule 36 admits by silence, could concede the matter.
== WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED ====================================
(1) ANY BACKWARD ROW. Rule 6(a) addresses only a period that `begins to
run` after an act -- there is no backward provision -- so
sc_rcp_6's rollover_suffix_backward is blank. Rule 6(d)'s TEN-day
motion notice and TWO-day affidavit periods are both backward and are
therefore absent, even though the two-day period is the one row that
would actually exercise the seven-day exclusion.
(2) THE POST-CONVICTION-RELIEF PERIODS in Rule 12(a) -- the State answers
an application within 60 days if it arises out of a guilty plea and 90
days if out of a trial. Criminal-adjacent, party-specific, and
reachable only in PCR proceedings.
(3) Rule 12(a)'s motion-tolling limbs.
(4) Appellate rows (SCACR is a separate body of rules).
== RULE 6(b)'s NO-ENLARGEMENT LIST, RECORDED =========================
Rule 6(b) names the rules whose time may NOT be extended -- 50(b), 52(b),
59, 60(b) -- and adds: `The time for filing notice of intent to appeal is
jurisdictional and may not be extended by consent or order.` None is
seeded here, but a future row under any of them must never carry an
enlargement note.
== NOT MODELLED, ALL EARLY, DISCLOSED =================================
Rule 6(a)'s `A half holiday shall be considered as other days and not as a
holiday` -- inert today, since nothing in § 53-5-10 is a half holiday, but
it is the rule pre-emptively refusing a category and is recorded rather
than dropped. Rules 33, 34 and 36 carry court-order escapes (`unless the
court shortens the time`, `unless the court directs otherwise`) the engine
cannot see.
Rule 4 (service of process) was not read, so what date a caller supplies
for `service of the summons and complaint` is not sourced from the rule
text. Rule 12(a)'s reference to `Rule 4(e)` -- where the court may direct
otherwise -- was likewise not read.

rules.label: Answer after service of the complaint (South Carolina)

authority.quote: A defendant shall serve his answer within 30 days after the service of the complaint upon him, unless the Court directs otherwise when service of process is made pursuant to Rule 4(e),
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, AND THE TRIGGER IS SERVICE OF THE COMPLAINT rather than of the summons and complaint together — the rule says 'the complaint', and the discovery rules three rules later say 'the summons and complaint', so the two are named differently and are not interchangeable. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: Rule 6(e) reaches 'a notice or other paper', and a complaint is process. 'Unless the Court directs otherwise when service of process is made pursuant to Rule 4(e)' is an override the engine cannot see, and Rule 4(e) was not read. NOT SEEDED from the same sentence: the post-conviction-relief periods, where the State answers within 60 days if the application arises out of a guilty plea and 90 days if out of a trial — criminal-adjacent, party-specific, and reachable only in PCR proceedings.

authority.quote: A party served with a pleading stating a cross-claim against him shall serve an answer thereto within 30 days after the service upon him.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS. THE SERVICE EXTENSION APPLIES HERE and not on the answer-to-complaint row: a pleading stating a crossclaim is a paper served between parties, which is what Rule 6(e) reaches, where the complaint is process.

service_extension.note: FIVE days, not three — Rule 6(e)'s own drafting Note says the federal three was 'increased from 3 to 5 days'. Carrying a neighbour's three computes TWO DAYS EARLY. It also reaches SERVICE UPON A STATUTORY AGENT, which no other seeded rule does. E-MAIL IS NOT LISTED, deliberately: whether the five days reach e-mail is unresolved on the primary sources read, and adding them would compute LATE if wrong. See the file readme.

rules.label: Reply to a counterclaim in the answer (South Carolina)

authority.quote: The plaintiff shall serve his reply to a counterclaim in the answer within 30 days after service of the answer or, if a reply is ordered by the court, within 30 days after service of the order, unless the order otherwise directs.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS FROM SERVICE OF THE ANSWER containing the counterclaim. The sentence carries a SECOND limb — thirty days after service of a court ORDER where a reply is ordered — not seeded as its own row because it is reachable only when such an order exists and would be indistinguishable by trigger date alone; a caller in that position should supply the order's service date here and read the citation. 'Unless the order otherwise directs' is an override the engine cannot see. The extension applies: an answer is a paper served between parties.

rules.label: Answers and objections to interrogatories (South Carolina)

authority.quote: shall serve a copy of the answers, and objections if any, within 30 days after the service of the interrogatories, except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, and the 45-day defendant provision is PERMISSIVE — 'a defendant MAY serve' — running from a DIFFERENT EVENT. It is therefore a SEPARATE PLAIN ROW rather than a floor, and the engine never chooses between them: choosing would need both dates AND a party-role field, and there is none. CONTRAST RULE 36 THREE RULES LATER, whose 45 days are 'shall not be required' — a mandatory floor, encoded as a later_of. The two wordings are close enough to read across and mean opposite things: treating this one as a floor would compute LATE for a defendant who did not take the alternative.

rules.label: Interrogatory answers — DEFENDANT's 45-day alternative, running from service of the summons and complaint (South Carolina)

authority.quote: except that a defendant may serve answers or objections within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant.
authority.note: A DIFFERENT CLOCK FROM A DIFFERENT EVENT, AND AN OPTION RATHER THAN A REPLACEMENT — 'a defendant MAY serve'. Where both are available the defendant relies on whichever they choose, and choosing requires knowing both dates and that the party is a defendant; the engine has no party-role field and does not decide. Structured identically to Georgia's O.C.G.A. 9-11-33(a)(2) and Florida's Rule 1.340(a)(9). NO SERVICE EXTENSION: this clock starts on service of the SUMMONS AND COMPLAINT, which is process, and Rule 6(e) reaches 'a notice or other paper'. Note the trigger names the summons AND complaint, where the Rule 12(a) answer row names the complaint alone — the rules word it differently and the triggers are not interchangeable.

rules.label: Response to a request for production (South Carolina)

authority.quote: The party upon whom the request is served shall serve a written response within 30 days after the service of the request, except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, structured identically to Rule 33 including the PERMISSIVE 45-day defendant alternative, which is again its own row. See the Rule 33 row for why 'may serve' is not a floor and Rule 36's 'shall not be required' is.

authority.quote: except that a defendant may serve a response within 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon that defendant.
authority.note: Separate row for the same reason as the Rule 33 alternative: a different clock from a different event, permissive rather than automatic, and the engine does not choose. NO SERVICE EXTENSION — the clock starts on service of process. The trigger name is distinct from the Rule 33 one on purpose: they are the same event in fact, but a shared trigger would put two rules in force at once, which the engine refuses as AMBIGUOUS_RULE.

rules.label: Response to requests for admission (South Carolina) — SILENCE ADMITS

authority.quote: addressed to the matter, signed by the party or by his attorney, but, unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon him.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS FOR A PARTY WHO IS NOT A DEFENDANT, or a defendant whose 45-day floor has passed. A DEFENDANT SHOULD USE THE later-of ROW — relying on this one alone can produce a date up to 45 days too early, and under Rule 36 silence ADMITS, so that does not merely mislead. The quote is the tail of the sentence, which is where the floor sits; the thirty days and the admit-by-silence framing are earlier in the same subsection. NOTE THE WORDING: 'shall not be required' is a MANDATORY FLOOR, unlike Rules 33 and 34's 'a defendant MAY serve', which are permissive alternatives with their own rows. Georgia has the identical split three sections apart.

rules.label: Requests for admission — DEFENDANT, the later of 30 days and the 45-day floor (South Carolina)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the request
45 days after service of the summons and complaint

authority.quote: unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 45 days after service of the summons and complaint upon him.
authority.note: A MANDATORY FLOOR, NOT AN ELECTION — 'shall not be required', where Rules 33 and 34 say 'a defendant MAY serve'. That difference is the whole reason this row is a resolve_periods and those two are plain rows. TWO LIMBS WITH DIFFERENT COUNTS (30 from the request, 45 from the summons and complaint), so this is resolve_periods and not the plain resolve: later_of that shares one count. Georgia's O.C.G.A. 9-11-36(a)(2) was first encoded as an ordinary later_of and shipped FIFTEEN DAYS EARLY, which is why the shape exists. THE ENGINE REFUSES UNLESS BOTH DATES ARE SUPPLIED. Both limbs run from caller-supplied dates, so South Carolina does not hit the Maryland chained-floor gap. 'Unless the court shortens the time' is an order the engine cannot see. NO SERVICE EXTENSION ON THIS ROW: no seeded rule combines resolve_periods with one, and inventing the interaction would be guessing at an order no rule text settles.
